problems.title: Bulk modulus of a glass-filled epoxy
problems.setup: An epoxy potting compound for a deep-ocean sensor housing uses matrix A (E = 3.0 GPa, ν = 0.35) filled with solid glass spheres B (E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.22) at volume fraction f = 0.3. The part is loaded by hydrostatic pressure p, so σ = −pI.

parts.ask: Define the bulk modulus from a hydrostatic test and find K_A for the neat epoxy.
sol: Hydrostatic stress σ = −pI gives volume strain e = tr ε = ΔV/V
K = −p/e; Hooke's law gives K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) = λ + 2μ/3

parts.ask: At about 4000 m depth, p = 40 MPa. Find ΔV/V of the neat epoxy, in percent.
Assume both phases carry the same pressure p (uniform stress). Find K_eff.
sol: Volume strains add by volume fraction: e = −p[(1 − f)/K_A + f/K_B]

parts.ask: Now assume both phases share the same volume strain (uniform strain). Find K_eff.
sol: Pressures add by volume fraction: K_eff = (1 − f)K_A + fK_B

parts.ask: Where does the true K_eff lie relative to these two estimates?
parts.a: Between them: uniform pressure (4.61 GPa) is the Reuss lower bound and uniform strain (15.19 GPa) is the Voigt upper bound
w: Above 15.19 GPa: uniform pressure is the upper bound because both phases share p equally
Exactly 4.61 GPa: uniform pressure is exact for a hydrostatic load
Below 4.61 GPa: interface shear softens the composite below both estimates
sol: Uniform stress meets equilibrium but breaks compatibility at the interfaces: complementary energy gives a lower bound
Uniform strain meets compatibility but breaks interface equilibrium: potential energy gives an upper bound
Stiff particles make the gap wide; the Hashin-Shtrikman bounds tighten it to 5.09 to 10.53 GPa

problems.x: The uniform pressure estimate 1/K_eff = (1 − f)/K_A + f/K_B is the Reuss lower bound, and the uniform strain average is the Voigt upper bound.

problems.title: Rubber bearing in finite simple shear
problems.setup: A rubber bearing pad (incompressible neo-Hookean, W = (μ/2)(I₁ − 3), μ = 0.4 MPa) is bonded between two rigid plates with normal e₂. The pad is h = 20 mm thick with a plate area of 100 mm by 100 mm. The top plate slides u = 10 mm along e₁, so x₁ = X₁ + γX₂, x₂ = X₂, x₃ = X₃. The faces normal to e₃ are traction free. Use σ = −pI + μB with B = FFᵀ.

parts.ask: What is γ, and what does it measure?
parts.a: γ = u/h = 0.5 = tan θ, the tangent of the angle through which vertical material lines tilt
w: γ = θ = 0.5 rad, the tilt angle itself
γ = u/h = 0.5 is the Green shear strain E₁₂
γ = 2u/h = 1.0, twice the tensor shear strain
sol: The line X₁ = 0 maps to x₁ = γx₂, so tan θ = γ = 10/20 = 0.5 (θ = 26.6°)

parts.ask: Find the shear force the top plate must apply.
sol: σ₁₂ = μγ = 0.4 · 0.5 = 0.2 MPa, exactly linear in γ, so τ/μ = γ

parts.ask: Use the traction-free faces to find the pressure p.
sol: p = μ = 0.4 MPa (the constraint pressure comes from a boundary condition)

parts.ask: Find the normal stress σ₁₁.
sol: σ₂₂ = −p + μ = 0, so the plates need zero normal force

parts.ask: Why does σ₁₁ appear, and what does linear elasticity give for it?
parts.a: It comes from the γ² term in B₁₁ = 1 + γ², a second-order effect of finite shear. It is even in γ, so reversing the shear keeps it tensile, and at γ = 0.5 it is already half the shear stress. Linear elasticity keeps only terms linear in γ, so it predicts σ₁₁ = 0 and is accurate only while γ² is small compared with γ.
sol: σ₁₁ − σ₂₂ = μγ²: the Poynting (normal stress) effect
Holding pure simple shear needs a tension μγ² on the faces normal to e₁

problems.x: In finite simple shear of a neo-Hookean solid σ₁₂ = μγ, and a normal stress difference σ₁₁ − σ₂₂ = μγ² appears at second order.

problems.title: Spinning flywheel disc: solid versus bored
problems.setup: A thin steel flywheel disc (ρ = 7800 kg/m³, ν = 0.3) of outer radius b = 250 mm spins at 6000 rpm with a free rim, in plane stress. General solution: σ_rr = A − B/r² − ((3 + ν)/8)ρω²r², σ_θθ = A + B/r² − ((1 + 3ν)/8)ρω²r².

parts.ask: Which radial equilibrium equation does this general solution satisfy?
w: dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r − ρω²r = 0
dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0, with ρω²r applied as a rim load
dσ_rr/dr + (σ_θθ − σ_rr)/r + ρω²r = 0
sol: The centrifugal body force ρω²r points outward and adds to the radial balance
A ± B/r² is the homogeneous Lamé part
The r² terms are the particular solution forced by ρω²r

parts.ask: Solid disc: find the stress at the centre, where σ_rr = σ_θθ.
sol: Finite stress at r = 0 needs B = 0

parts.ask: Solid disc: find the hoop stress at the rim.
A central bore of radius a = 25 mm is machined (free surface). Find the hoop stress at the bore.
sol: σ_rr(a) = σ_rr(b) = 0 gives A = ((3 + ν)/8)ρω²(a² + b²), B = ((3 + ν)/8)ρω²a²b²

parts.ask: As the bore radius a shrinks toward zero, what does the bore hoop stress approach?
parts.a: Twice the solid disc centre stress, ((3 + ν)/4)ρω²b²: a pinhole is a stress concentration of 2
w: The solid disc centre stress, as the hole effect fades with a
Three times the solid centre stress, as for a hole in a plate under uniaxial tension
Zero, since the bore surface is traction free
sol: Bore: ((3 + ν)/4)ρω²b² as a → 0; solid centre: ((3 + ν)/8)ρω²b²
The solid centre is equibiaxial, and a hole in an equibiaxial field has K_t = 2

problems.x: A spinning disc needs the particular solution driven by ρω²r, and a small central bore doubles the peak hoop stress of the solid disc.

problems.title: Thick-walled helium sphere: Lamé with 1/r³
problems.setup: A spherical helium tank for a launch vehicle has inner radius a = 100 mm, outer radius b = 125 mm, internal pressure p = 60 MPa and zero external pressure. Use the spherically symmetric Lamé solution.

parts.ask: Which stress field applies to the thick sphere?
parts.a: σ_rr = A − 2B/r³, σ_θθ = σ_φφ = A + B/r³
w: σ_rr = A − B/r², σ_θθ = A + B/r², as for the thick cylinder
An Airy function in polar coordinates, φ = A ln r + Br²
σ_rr = A − B/r³, σ_θθ = σ_φφ = A + B/r³
sol: Spherical symmetry: u = u(r), with u = Cr + D/r²
Airy is a plane construct; the sphere is a 3D problem

parts.ask: Find the hoop stress at the bore, σ_θθ(a).
sol: A = pa³/(b³ − a³) = 62.95 MPa, B = pa³b³/(2(b³ − a³))

parts.ask: The bore is equibiaxial plus radial. Find the von Mises stress there.
sol: Principal stresses at the bore: (124.4, 124.4, −60) MPa
σ_vm = √(½[(σ_θ − σ_φ)² + (σ_φ − σ_r)² + (σ_r − σ_θ)²]) = σ_θ − σ_r

parts.ask: Find the thin-wall estimate pr_m/(2t) using the mean radius.
sol: t/r_m = 0.22 is outside the thin-wall range (about 0.1), and the thin-wall model drops σ_rr = −p at the bore

parts.ask: Twist: a long closed-end cylinder has the same a, b and p. Find its bore hoop stress.
sol: Lamé cylinder: σ_θθ(a) = p(b² + a²)/(b² − a²)
About 2.2 times the sphere: the sphere carries p with two hoop directions

problems.x: A thick sphere uses the 1/r³ Lamé solution, and its bore carries an equibiaxial hoop stress plus the radial stress −p.

problems.title: Free inclined edge: traction condition to principal stress
problems.setup: A thin aluminium wing skin (plane stress) has a straight cut edge with outward unit normal n = (cos 120°, sin 120°) = (−1/2, √3/2). At a point on that edge a strain rosette gives σ₁₁ = 60 MPa. The edge carries zero load.

parts.ask: What boundary condition does the free edge impose?
parts.a: t = σn = 0: both traction components vanish on the inclined edge
w: σ₁₁ = 0 and σ₁₂ = 0, the components on an x₁ face
σ₂₂ = 0 alone, since the edge faces mostly upward
n·σn = 0 alone; a shear traction can remain
sol: An edge oblique to the axes mixes all three components
t₁ = σ₁₁n₁ + σ₁₂n₂ = 0 and t₂ = σ₁₂n₁ + σ₂₂n₂ = 0

parts.ask: Find σ₁₂ at the edge point (2 decimals).
Find σ₂₂.
Find the largest principal stress (here it also equals the von Mises stress).
sol: σ₁ = 80 MPa, σ₂ = 0: the circle touches the origin and the edge normal is a principal direction
The state is uniaxial along the edge tangent (30°), so σ_vm = 80 MPa

parts.ask: Twist: a clamp presses the edge with uniform pressure q = 10 MPa (t = −qn), and σ₁₁ = 60 MPa still. Find the largest principal stress (2 decimals).
sol: σn = −qn: n is a principal direction with principal stress −10 MPa

problems.x: On an inclined boundary the traction condition is t = σn, and on a free or uniformly pressed edge it makes the edge normal a principal direction carrying the applied normal traction.

problems.title: Inverse Airy problem with a quartic stress function
problems.setup: A thin rectangular panel occupies 0 ≤ x ≤ L, −c ≤ y ≤ c (unit thickness, plane stress) with L = 0.5 m and c = 0.1 m. The trial stress function is φ = B(x²y² − y⁴/3) with B = 20 MPa/m². Use σ_xx = φ,yy, σ_yy = φ,xx, σ_xy = −φ,xy.

parts.ask: Is φ an admissible Airy function, and what does the check enforce?
parts.a: Yes: ∇⁴φ = 0 + 2(4B) − 8B = 0, which enforces compatibility; equilibrium holds automatically
w: Yes: ∇⁴φ = 0 enforces equilibrium, and compatibility holds automatically
No: φ,yyyy = −8B is nonzero, so ∇⁴φ is nonzero
Yes: every polynomial stress function is biharmonic

parts.ask: Find σ_xy at (x, y) = (0.25 m, 0.1 m).
Find the normal traction on the face y = +c.
sol: At y = c: 2 · 20 · 0.01 = 0.4 MPa, uniform tension along the face
The face also carries shear t₁ = σ_xy = −4Bcx, linear in x

parts.ask: Find the axial force resultant on the end x = L, in kN per m of thickness.
sol: N = ∫ σ_xx dy from −c to c = B(4L²c − 8c³/3)

parts.ask: A candidate writes σ_xy = +φ,xy. What goes wrong?
w: Nothing: the shear sign is a convention
Compatibility fails, so ∇⁴φ changes
The face tractions flip sign while equilibrium still holds
sol: The minus sign in σ_xy = −φ,xy makes the two terms cancel

problems.x: The Airy definitions with σ_xy = −φ,xy satisfy equilibrium identically, and ∇⁴φ = 0 supplies compatibility.
